source.title: A New Look at Ghost Normalization

record.tranche_reason: The study tests how GhostNorm and SeqNorm affect held-out image-classification accuracy and measures loss-landscape smoothness, using different interventions and measures from the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports validation and test accuracy for normalization variants and qualitative loss-landscape comparisons. It does not measure train error, fit random labels, sweep model width or training batch size, test dropout, or measure magnitude-aware sharpness. Its generalization results do not directly test a listed version.
record.test_reason: The study compares normalization methods and gradient-direction loss smoothness, but tests none of V1–V8. Optimization batch size is fixed within comparisons, so changing normalization group size does not test V5. Gradient predictiveness does not measure V7's magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance or its association with generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion: GhostNorm can improve generalization despite reducing measured loss-landscape smoothness, and selected SeqNorm configurations outperform the reported BatchNorm and GhostNorm baselines. This is not uniform across configurations: CIFAR-100 GhostNorm GM=2 has lower test accuracy than BatchNorm. The authors also propose a regularization mechanism and a sequential tuning strategy.
record.recipe_differences: Tests normalization interventions (GhostNorm and SeqNorm) and qualitative loss-landscape smoothness, not the interventions or measures in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies with normalization type and its group settings (GM, GC); the loss-landscape smoothness change is visible only toward later epochs on CIFAR–10.

fits_no_version.finding: GhostNorm reduces gradient-direction loss smoothness relative to BatchNorm on MNIST and, late in training, CIFAR-10. The authors report better generalization in almost all experiments, but this is not a magnitude-aware sharpness–gap comparison.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: GhostNorm can improve held-out performance while reducing gradient-direction loss smoothness.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed optimization batch of 512, selected GhostNorm and SeqNorm configurations improve test accuracy over the BatchNorm baseline: 82.8% and 83.8% versus 82.1% on CIFAR-100, and 97.3% and 97.4% versus 97.1% on CIFAR-10. CIFAR-100 GhostNorm GM=2 instead reaches 81.2%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalization choice and grouping can change held-out accuracy at fixed optimization batch size; selected SeqNorm configurations outperform the tested baselines.

record.problems: The reported accuracy averages are based on two runs, but dispersion or error bars are not given. The study does not report training error, so train/test gaps cannot be compared. The authors say some negative preliminary experiments were omitted and that more tuning might change their outcomes.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Matched convolutional versus fully connected comparisons and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under specified tuning budgets.
Held-out performance across optimization batch sizes at fixed epoch budgets, including whether recipe adaptations remove a batch-size penalty.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on dataset size, augmentation, or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps at similarly low training loss, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: R3–R9 report the study's own normalization-method performance and should not be treated as eligible evidence for V1–V8. The batch-size increase from 128 to 512 describes adaptation of a borrowed recipe, not a measured small-versus-large-batch comparison. All row states are therefore cannot_determine relative to the listed versions, rather than judgments about whether the reported normalization effects occurred.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width beyond the interpolation threshold and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Training batch-size effects at fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects and its interaction with weight decay or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures, and correlations among networks at similar training loss.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.

rows.subject: SimpleNet
rows.size_stated: two fully-connected layers of 512 and 300 neurons
rows.operation_detail: Compared loss-landscape smoothness during training for BatchNorm, GhostNorm, and no normalization.
rows.measure: Qualitative loss-landscape smoothness, assessed by gradient predictiveness across learning rates.
rows.value: GhostNorm loss landscape bears closer resemblance to the no-normalization baseline; authors report smoothness deteriorates with GhostNorm.
rows.note: No numerical smoothness values or train/test error gap are reported.
rows.check: The qualitative smoothness finding is correctly described, but cannot establish any listed version, including V7.

rows.subject: ResNet–56
rows.operation_detail: Compared loss-landscape smoothness during training for BatchNorm, GhostNorm, and no normalization.
rows.measure: Qualitative loss-landscape smoothness, assessed by gradient predictiveness across cyclical learning rates.
rows.value: GhostNorm loss-landscape smoothness deteriorates, observable toward the last epochs of training.
rows.note: Authors locate the difference toward the last epochs; no numerical smoothness values or train/test error gap are reported.
rows.check: The late-training smoothness deterioration is correctly described. Its timing does not make it a partial observation of V7; the measure differs from magnitude-aware sharpness.

rows.subject: Wide-ResNet models of 28 depth and 10 width
rows.operation_detail: Trained with BatchNorm; reported validation and test accuracy.
rows.uncertainty: Performances averaged over two different runs; variance not stated.
rows.note: The paper states results are averaged over two runs.
rows.check: Accuracy values agree with Table 1, but this is a comparator for the study's normalization method, not evidence for a listed version. BatchNorm uses unsynchronized statistics across eight GPUs, equivalent to global GhostNorm GM=8.

rows.subject: Wide-ResNet models of 28 depth and 10 width
rows.operation_detail: Trained with GhostNorm, GM = 2; reported validation and test accuracy.
rows.uncertainty: Performances averaged over two different runs; variance not stated.
rows.note: Test accuracy is lower than the BatchNorm comparator.
rows.check: The reported normalization comparison does not test a listed version. Test accuracy falls from 82.1% to 81.2%; calling this partial has no basis in V1–V8. GM=2 is applied per GPU, equivalent to global GM=16.

rows.subject: Wide-ResNet models of 28 depth and 10 width
rows.operation_detail: Trained with GhostNorm, GM = 8; reported validation and test accuracy.
rows.uncertainty: Performances averaged over two different runs; variance not stated.
rows.note: Authors state GhostNorm improves over the baseline by 0.7%; the table reports the accuracy values.
rows.check: The accuracy improvement is a result for the study's normalization method, not a listed version. GM=8 on eight GPUs is equivalent to global GM=64; the optimization batch remains 512.

rows.subject: Wide-ResNet models of 28 depth and 10 width
rows.operation_detail: Trained with SeqNorm, GC = 4 and GM = 8; reported validation and test accuracy.
rows.uncertainty: Performances averaged over two different runs; variance not stated.
rows.note: Authors state SeqNorm improves upon the baseline by 1.7%.
rows.check: The accuracy improvement evaluates SeqNorm rather than a listed version. GM=8 is per GPU, equivalent to global GM=64.

rows.subject: Wide-ResNet models of 28 depth and 10 width
rows.operation_detail: Trained with BatchNorm; reported validation and test accuracy.
rows.uncertainty: Performances averaged over two different runs; variance not stated.
rows.note: The paper states results are averaged over two runs.
rows.check: Accuracy values agree with Table 2, but this is a normalization-method comparator. BatchNorm uses unsynchronized statistics across eight GPUs, equivalent to global GhostNorm GM=8.

rows.subject: Wide-ResNet models of 28 depth and 10 width
rows.operation_detail: Trained with GhostNorm, GM = 4; reported validation and test accuracy.
rows.uncertainty: Performances averaged over two different runs; variance not stated.
rows.note: The test-accuracy improvement over BatchNorm is small; the paper reports similar validation performance for GM values 2, 4, and 8.
